textbookText: Functions The liver performs the following important functions: i. It secretes green coloured alkaline bile juice containing bile salts, bile pigments, cholesterol, water etc. Bile juice reduces acidity of food, provides suitable medium for the activation of pancreatic enzymes and emulsifies fats. Conversion of larger fat globules into smaller forms by the action of bile juice is called emulsification. ii. Liver is an important organ of metabolism of carbohydrate, protein and fats. Glucose absorbed from the wall of alimentary canal, if excess, is converted to glycogen by the process of glycogenesis in liver. Similarly, glycogen may be converted to glucose, if required, by the process of glycogenolysis. Formation of new glucose (gluconeogenesis) from non-carbohydrate compounds such as amino acid and glycerol also takes place in liver. iii. Liver performs the function of de-amination and detoxification. As the amino acids can’t be stored in the body of animals, metabolism of amino acid produces ammonia as by-product, called deamination. Ammonia is highly toxic, reacts with carbon dioxide in liver to convert into less toxic urea by the process of detoxification. iv. It also removes some other excretory products such as bilirubin and biliverdin formed by break down of old RBCs, which are discharged with bile into the intestine and expelled with the faeces. v. In an embryo, RBCs are formed in liver but in an adult old and worn out RBCs are destroyed in liver. vi. Kupffer cells are the phagocytic cells which destroy harmful microbes such as bacteria. vii. It stores copper and iron and fat-soluble vitamins. viii. Fibrinogen and prothrombin are synthesized in liver which are essential blood clotting factors. ix. Liver also secretes heparin which prevents clotting of blood in blood vessels.

2. Pancreas: It is an irregularly branched, flat and cream coloured gland of exocrine and endocrine nature, which is held in position by mesentery between the stomach and duodenum. It is traversed by the common bile duct into which the ducts from pancreas also open to from a hepatopancreatic duct. Histologically, exocrine part of pancreas consists of many pancreatic lobules or acini embedded in connective tissues. Connective tissue also contains pancreatic ducts, blood vessels, lymph vessels and nerves. Each acinus consists of secretory cells of columnar type around a central cavity or lumen. Secretory cells are with a large nucleus and filled with non-granular cytoplasm. These cells secrete pancreatic juice containing digestive enzymes which is poured into central lumen or ductule. Acini unite with each other through their ductules, which in turn unite to form the larger ducts and finally form the pancreatic ducts. The pancreatic ducts open into the bile duct from liver to form hepatopancreatic duct.

Figure 8.4.12 T.S. of pancreas of frog Similarly, Endocrine Part consists of a compact group of specialised cells in the connective tissue amongst the acini, known as pancreatic islets or islets of Langerhans. The cells in islets are chiefly alpha Cells, beta Cells and delta Cells which secrete hormones which are directly poured into blood capillaries.
